newsitem.title: FRANCE: New poll confirms left catching up in French vote.
newsitem.headline: New poll confirms left catching up in French vote.

text.p: A second opinion poll in 24 hours showed on Sunday French left-wing parties catching up on the ruling centre-right majority ahead of a May 25-June 1 general election.

The poll, to be published in the conservative daily Le Figaro, showed the left heading to win 262 seats and the centre-right 291 from the 555 in metropolitan France. The poll did not take into account 22 seats in overseas territories.
The same SOFRES poll conducted a week ago gave the left 225 seats and the centre-right 329. The latest poll was conducted on Friday and Saturday among 1,000 adults.
The extreme rightist National Front, credited a week ago with one seat, was predicted to get two according to the most recent poll.

The FN is predicted to get 15 percent of the vote but France's two-round electoral system favours established mainstream parties who can make between-rounds agreements which exclude fringe and extremist groups from parliamentary life.
The latest poll showed 35 percent of voters said they could still change their minds while a further 19 percent did not reply.
A separate poll, published earlier in the newspaper Le Journal du Dimanche, had earlier shown the rise in pro-left votes.
The publication of the two polls injected new excitement into the election campaign which officially opens on Monday and has so far failed to drum up much public enthusiasm.

Le Journal du Dimanche noted that if the left outstripped the right at the polls, the situation would be far from smooth for the new majority, which would have to cohabit uneasily with President Jacques Chirac for the remaining five years of his seven-year term in office.
The left's main force, the Socialists, would also be at the mercy of their uneasy Communist and ecologist allies if they wanted to stay in power.
The conservative daily Le Figaro said Chirac, always a highly effective campaigner, would intervene in the campaign on Wednesday to shore up his faltering backers.
This was denied by his office but Prime Minister Alain Juppe said he would consider it normal for Chirac to intervene.

Political leaders have already started to criss-cross the country to hold meetings, but there is wide agreement the campaign has been bland with much blame going to Juppe and Socialist opposition chief Lionel Jospin, leaders of their respective camps.

Opinion polls show the French at large would have preferred former European Commission president Jacques Delors as leader of the left instead of Jospin, often seen as a lacklustre intellectual out of touch with everyday public concerns.
The dry Juppe is the most unpopular prime minister in nearly 40 years, with opinion polls showing the public often describing him as arrogant and unlikeable.
Dozens of youths gathered on Friday night outside a restaurant in Bordeaux, where he is mayor, to throw eggs and water-filled bags at him as he emerged.
Philippe de Villiers, who opposes links with the European Union, launched his campaign on Sunday, proposing that his Movement for France turn the election into "a referendum (against) Europe".
De Villiers, with Anglo-French financier Jimmy Goldsmith then on his list, won a surprising 12 percent in elections to the European Parliament in 1994.

Socialist former Industry minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, denying his party was vague about costs of election promises in case of victory, said creating jobs for 700,000 youths would cost 22 to 23 billion francs ($3.78 billion to $3.95) billion.
Former Socialist Culture Minister Jack Lang called on Chirac to reopen electoral lists to allow 800,000 unregistered youths to sign on to vote for the first time.

Five members of extreme-rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front party were slightly hurt when they were attacked by about 20 ultra-leftists while handing out leaflets at an open-air market in the northern city of Lille, police said.
Le Pen is to hold an election rally in Lille on Wednesday.
